name: Novaril
description: Novaril is Novafold's attempt at a comprehensive cognitive enhancement platform — a stack of carefully balanced compounds that elevates working memory, processing speed, attention, and recall simultaneously without the jagged edges of single-function enhancers. It is the 'safe' option: lower ceiling, lower risk, designed for daily use by people who need to be reliably better without being dangerously better. Marketed aggressively to Tier 3 professionals as a subscription wellness product.
effects: Moderate, reliable elevation across all cognitive domains
Reduced cognitive fatigue over the course of a workday
Smoother BCI integration and interface responsiveness
Mild mood stabilization — reduced anxiety interference with performance
side_effects: Cognitive ceiling effect — users cannot exceed the drug's moderate enhancement level regardless of dose
Tolerance builds within weeks, requiring cycling
Discontinuation produces a below-baseline cognitive slump lasting 1-2 weeks
Some users report emotional flattening — competent but less emotionally present
cultural_context: Novaril is aspirational consumption — the drug you take when you've made it to Tier 3 and want to stay there. Novafold sells it on subscription with automatic renewal, with a slick app that tracks your 'cognitive performance metrics' and recommends dosage adjustments. The subscription model is the point: Novaril users who cycle off experience a slump that feels like cognitive decline but is actually just the return of baseline, and they re-subscribe immediately. Tier 3 social circles have developed a quiet stigma around not being on Novaril — it signals either poverty (can't afford the subscription) or eccentricity (choosing not to optimize). On the Shelf, stolen or counterfeit Novaril tablets circulate, prized because they're one of the few cognitive enhancers with a tolerable side effect profile.
story_hooks: Novafold's performance tracking app has been quietly building a comprehensive cognitive map of its entire user base — the data is worth more than the drug, and someone inside the company is preparing to sell it to an interested third party.

The 'below-baseline slump' that Novaril users experience during discontinuation is not a natural withdrawal effect — it's an engineered dependency built into the formula, and a rogue Novafold chemist has the proof.

A Tier 3 manager has been secretly off Novaril for three months and is performing just as well as before — they're hiding it because admitting the drug does nothing for them would raise questions about why they've been billing it to their corporate wellness account.
